quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: Ten quick checks on creels, warper's beams, weaver's beams and the words used in warping production.

questions.q: A sized weaver's beam is made from:
options: Several warper's beams run together on the sizing machine
Several loom beams joined end to end
Cones taken straight from the creel
questions.explain: The warper can only wind as many ends as the creel has cones, so the total warp is split over several warper's beams which are combined into one weaver's beam at the sizing machine.

questions.q: What limits the number of ends that can be put on one warper's beam?
options: The number of cones the creel can hold
questions.explain: Each end needs its own cone on the creel; with a creel of 840 cones, a warper's beam can carry at most 840 ends.

questions.q: Why is the number of warper's beams rounded up to an even number?
options: Because looms always take two beams
Because beams are paired on the sizing creel
Because the warper runs two beams at once
Because an odd number of beams cannot be sized
questions.explain: Warper's beams are arranged in pairs on the sizing creel, so the total is rounded up to the next even number: 4.55 beams becomes 6, not 5.

questions.q: The total ends used for beam calculations include the extra selvedge ends.
questions.explain: Selvedge ends have to be warped and sized like any other end, so they are added to EPI × width before dividing by the creel capacity (3,780 + 40 = 3,820 for fabric A).

questions.q: In the worksheet, 'ends per beam (average)' for fabric A is 636.67. In practice this becomes:
options: 2 beams of 636 and 4 beams of 637 ends
3 beams of 636 and 3 beams of 637 ends
questions.explain: A beam cannot carry a fraction of an end, so the 3,820 ends are shared as 2 × 636 + 4 × 637 = 3,820. Six beams of 637 would give 3,822 and six of 636 only 3,816.

questions.q: Warping speed in the worksheet is measured in:
questions.explain: The warper's production is expressed as yards of warp wound per minute, which, multiplied by minutes per shift and efficiency, gives yards warped per shift.

questions.q: Which of these does NOT affect the weight of yarn warped in one shift?
questions.explain: Weight per shift = yards per shift × ends per beam ÷ (840 × Ne). Fabric width only enters earlier, in deciding how many ends and beams there are; once ends per beam are fixed it plays no part.

questions.q: The warp length required for an order equals the fabric length ordered, because the warp runs straight through the loom.
questions.explain: The warp crimps over the picks, so the warp must be longer than the fabric by the warp contraction: 21,872 yd of fabric A needs 24,059 yd of warp at 10 % contraction.

questions.q: Efficiency in the warping production worksheet accounts for:
options: Time the warper is stopped for creeling, piecing breaks and doffing
The difference between yards and metres
questions.explain: Efficiency is the fraction of shift time the warper actually runs; stops for creel changes, end breaks and beam changes reduce it, so yards per shift = speed × minutes × efficiency.

questions.q: The lecture notes that a 20,000 m order of fabric A keeps the warper busy for only about 4.3 hours. What is the point being made?
options: Warping is the slowest process in the mill
A single warper can serve one order easily; a whole loom shed needs more than one
The order should be warped on two warpers
Warping cannot be done in less than a shift
questions.explain: One order is a small load for a warper, but Lecture 10 shows that feeding 200 looms continuously needs more than one warper. The 4.3 hours is a fraction of one 8-hour shift.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: The beam and warping-production formulas, their units and the direction each input pushes the result.

questions.q: The number of warper's beams is found as:
questions.explain: beams = round-up-to-even(total ends ÷ creel capacity). Rounding down would leave ends with no cone; the ratio must also be inverted the right way round.

questions.q: If the creel capacity rises from 840 to 1,000 cones, the number of beams for a 3,820-end warp:
questions.explain: 3,820 ÷ 1,000 = 3.82, which rounds up to the even number 4. A bigger creel means fewer, fuller beams.

questions.q: Yards warped per shift equals:
questions.explain: Minutes in the shift = hours × 60, so yards = speed × hours × 60 × efficiency; forgetting the 60 understates the production 60 times. Ends per beam enter only when converting to weight.

questions.q: Weight warped per shift (lb) is:
options: yards per shift × ends per beam × 840 × Ne
yards per shift ÷ (ends per beam × 840 × Ne)
yards per shift × ends per beam ÷ (840 × Ne)
yards per shift ÷ ends per beam × 840 × Ne
questions.explain: Every yard of beam contains 'ends per beam' yards of yarn, and 840 × Ne yards weigh 1 lb, so weight = yards × ends ÷ (840 × Ne).

questions.q: With the same speed and ends per beam, warping a finer count gives a lower weight of yarn per shift.
questions.explain: Weight is proportional to 1 ÷ Ne; the same yardage of Ne 40 weighs half as much as Ne 20, so the pounds per shift fall even though the yards do not.

questions.q: Warp length required for an order equals:
options: fabric length in yards ÷ (1 + warp contraction)
fabric length in yards × (1 + warp contraction)
fabric length in metres × (1 + warp contraction)
fabric length in yards × warp contraction
questions.explain: Each yard of fabric uses (1 + contraction) yards of warp, so the warp must be 10 % longer at 10 % contraction; the lecture works in yards after converting metres × 1.0936.

questions.q: Warp weight required for an order (lb) is calculated from:
options: warp length × total ends in fabric ÷ (840 × Ne)
warp length × ends per beam ÷ (840 × Ne)
questions.explain: The whole warp must be weighed, so the total ends in the fabric (3,780 for A) are used, not the ends on one beam. The per-beam figure is used for the warper's production, not the order's weight.

questions.q: Warping time for an order in hours is:
options: warp weight required ÷ weight warped per hour
warp weight required × weight warped per hour
warp length required ÷ yards warped per shift
questions.explain: Time = pounds needed ÷ pounds per hour: 5,413 ÷ 1,273 ≈ 4.3 h. Dividing length by speed ignores that the warp is wound in several beams and that efficiency is below 100 %.

questions.q: If warping efficiency falls from 80 % to 60 % with everything else fixed, the warping time for an order:
questions.explain: Production is proportional to efficiency, so time is proportional to 1 ÷ efficiency: 80 ÷ 60 = 1.333, a rise of one third. A fall of 20 percentage points is not a 20 % change in time.

questions.q: Converting an order from metres to yards means multiplying by 0.9144.
questions.explain: A metre is longer than a yard: metres × 1.0936 = yards (20,000 m = 21,872 yd). Multiplying by 0.9144 goes the other way, yards to metres.

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Beam numbers, ends per beam and warping production worked through with realistic mill figures.

questions.q: A fabric has 72 ends per inch, is 60 inches wide and has 48 extra selvedge ends. How many ends must be warped in total?
A warp of 4,368 ends is to be made on a warper whose creel holds 840 cones. How many warper's beams are used (round up to an even number)?
questions.explain: 4,368 ÷ 840 = 5.2 beams; rounded up to the next even number this is 6 beams.

questions.q: If 4,368 ends are shared over 6 warper's beams, what is the average number of ends per beam?
questions.explain: 4,368 ÷ 6 = 728 ends per beam; in this case every beam can carry exactly the same number.

questions.q: Fabric B has 8,104 ends including selvedge and uses 10 beams. What is the average number of ends per beam (to one decimal place)?
questions.explain: 8,104 ÷ 10 = 810.4 ends; in practice 6 beams carry 810 and 4 carry 811 (6 × 810 + 4 × 811 = 8,104).

questions.q: A warper runs at 800 yd/min at 75 % efficiency on an 8-hour shift. How many yards are warped per shift?
A warper winds 288,000 yd per shift on beams of 700 ends of Ne 30. What weight of yarn is warped per shift, in lb?
An order is for 15,000 m of fabric. How many yards is this (to the nearest yard)?
16,404 yd of fabric is to be woven with 10 % warp contraction. What warp length must be warped (to the nearest yard)?
A warp 18,044 yd long has 4,320 ends of Ne 30. What is its weight in lb (to the nearest lb)?
An order needs 5,413 lb of warp and the warper produces 1,273 lb per hour. The warping time is closest to:
questions.explain: 5,413 ÷ 1,273 = 4.25 ≈ 4.3 hours, a little over half a shift. 0.24 is the reciprocal (1,273 ÷ 5,413).

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Planning-office situations: choosing the number of beams, loading the warper and judging whether an order fits the shift.

questions.q: A planner divides 3,820 ends by the 840-cone creel, gets 4.55 and orders 5 warper's beams. The sizing department objects. Why?
options: Beams are paired on the sizing creel, so an even number (6) is needed
The creel can only hold 4 beams' worth
5 beams would exceed the loom width
questions.explain: Five beams would hold 3,820 ends (764 each) but the sizing creel takes beams in pairs, so the lecture rounds up to the even number 6.

questions.q: With 6 beams of 636 or 637 ends on an 840-cone creel, roughly what fraction of the creel is in use?
questions.explain: 637 ÷ 840 = 0.76, so about a quarter of the creel positions stand empty. This is the cost of rounding up to an even number of beams.

questions.q: A mill wants to use its 840-cone creel more fully for fabric A (3,820 ends). Which change gets the ends per beam closest to the creel capacity while keeping an even number of beams?
questions.explain: 955 ends per beam is more than the 840 cones available, so 4 beams is impossible; 6 beams is the smallest even number that fits, giving 637 ends per beam. Eight beams would leave even more cones idle.

questions.q: The warper is scheduled for 268,800 yd per 8-hour shift at 80 % efficiency. On a bad day with many breaks efficiency drops to 60 %. Yards warped that shift are about:
questions.explain: At 100 % the warper would do 336,000 yd; at 60 % that is 201,600 yd (or 268,800 × 60 ÷ 80). 161,280 is 268,800 × 0.6, which applies the efficiency twice.

questions.q: If an order of 20,000 m of fabric A needs only 4.3 warping hours, the warper can be used for other orders during the rest of the shift.
questions.explain: The order fills about half of an 8-hour shift, so the remaining time is available; in practice warping capacity is planned for the whole loom shed, as Lecture 10 shows.

questions.q: A costing clerk calculates the warp weight for a 20,000 m order using the ends per beam (637) instead of the total ends (3,780). The result will be:
questions.explain: The order's warp has all 3,780 ends; using only one beam's share (637) gives roughly one sixth of the true 5,413 lb. The beam figure belongs in the warper's production calculation.

questions.q: Two orders of fabric A arrive, 20,000 m and 30,000 m. Warping time for both together on the same warper (4.3 h per 20,000 m) is about:
questions.explain: Time is proportional to length: 50,000 ÷ 20,000 × 4.25 h ≈ 10.6 hours, more than one shift. 6.4 h would be the 30,000 m order alone.

questions.q: A planner switches the warper from fabric A (Ne 20) to a fabric with the same ends per beam in Ne 40 at the same speed and efficiency. Pounds per shift will:
questions.explain: Yards per shift are unchanged, but Ne 40 yarn weighs half as much per yard as Ne 20, so 10,187 lb becomes about 5,094 lb per shift.

questions.q: The fabric is to be made 70" wide instead of 63" with the same 60 EPI and 40 selvedge ends. What happens to the beam plan on an 840-cone creel?
questions.explain: Total ends = 60 × 70 + 40 = 4,240; ÷ 840 = 5.05, rounded up to the even number 6; 4,240 ÷ 6 = 706.7 ends per beam, still within the 840-cone creel.

questions.q: Why does the lecture say that for a whole loom shed 'the picture changes'?
options: Because wider looms need more beams
Because 200 looms consume warp continuously and need more than one warper
Because a loom shed uses metres, not yards
Because efficiency falls when more looms are running
questions.explain: One order occupies the warper for a few hours, but keeping 200 looms supplied with beams all day needs more warping capacity than a single machine provides (Lecture 10).

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Harder questions across the lecture: multi-step beam and production reasoning and the mistakes that catch students out.

questions.q: A fabric has 96 EPI, is 66 inches wide and has 64 selvedge ends. The creel holds 1,000 cones. How many warper's beams are used (round up to even)?
questions.explain: Total ends = 96 × 66 + 64 = 6,400; ÷ 1,000 = 6.4, rounded up to the even number 8.

questions.q: A warper runs at 600 yd/min for an 8-hour shift at 85 % efficiency (244,800 yd per shift) on beams of 800 ends of Ne 40. What weight of yarn is warped per shift, in lb (to the nearest lb)?
A student computes beams for fabric B as 8,104 ÷ 840 = 9.65 and writes 'use 9 beams'. The two errors here are:
options: Rounding down, and forgetting to use an even number
Using the wrong creel capacity, and dividing instead of multiplying
Forgetting selvedge ends, and rounding down
Rounding up, and using an odd number
questions.explain: 9.65 must be rounded up (9 beams could not hold all the ends on an 840-cone creel) and then to an even number, giving 10. Selvedge ends are already included in 8,104.

questions.q: A 20,000 m order of fabric A (3,780 ends, Ne 20, 10 % warp contraction) needs 5,413 lb of warp. If 12.5 % size is to be added, what will the sized warp weigh in lb (to the nearest lb)?
questions.explain: Sized weight = 5,413 × 1.125 = 6,089.6 ≈ 6,090 lb. The size adds weight but no length (Lecture 8).

questions.q: Fabric A at 20,000 m needs 24,059 yd of warp on each of 6 beams. If a warper's beam can hold only 23,700 yd, what follows?
options: The order fits on one set of 6 beams
Each beam must be made in two lengths, or a second set of beams is needed
The order needs 12 cones per end
questions.explain: 24,059 yd per beam exceeds the beam's capacity of about 23,700 yd (Lecture 7), so the warp must be split into more than one set of beams; the number of cones per end is irrelevant.

questions.q: Doubling the warping speed halves the warping time for an order, provided the efficiency stays the same.
questions.explain: Yards per shift, and hence pounds per hour, are proportional to speed; at twice the speed the same pounds are warped in half the time. In practice faster running often lowers efficiency.

questions.q: The warper produces 10,187 lb per shift from 268,800 yd on 636.67-end beams of Ne 20. If the same yardage is warped on 810.4-end beams of Ne 20 (fabric B), the weight per shift is about:
questions.explain: Weight scales with ends per beam: 10,187 × 810.4 ÷ 636.67 = 12,967 lb (or 268,800 × 810.4 ÷ 16,800). More ends on the beam means more yarn wound per yard.

questions.q: An order of 12,000 m of fabric with 4,240 total ends of Ne 20 and 10 % warp contraction is to be warped. What warp weight in lb is required (to the nearest lb)?
Which of these would NOT reduce the number of warper's beams needed for a given fabric?
questions.explain: Beams depend on total ends ÷ creel capacity. Count affects the weight of the warp, not the number of ends, so a finer count leaves the beam count unchanged.

questions.q: A warper does 268,800 yd per shift. The same 3,820-end warp is planned as 6 beams of 24,059 yd. How many shifts of warper time does the full set of beams take, ignoring the time lost between beams?
questions.explain: 6 × 24,059 = 144,354 yd; ÷ 268,800 yd per shift = 0.54 shift, i.e. about 4.3 hours of an 8-hour shift, the same answer the weight route gives.
